doc.title: Konitz Lee — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: 'An Image' with Bill Russo's strings
summary: He liked the string quartet album with Russo and compares his comfort level with earlier records.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Yeah, An Image. Which actually, we segue neatly, I wanted to ask you the first record you did for Verve in fifty-eight is An Image with Russo which a lot of people think is one of your great records too. How do you feel about that one?
Bill wrote all of that music especially for you. Did you feel comfortable with the string quartet and the rhythm section?
So you felt more relaxed than some of the earlier records, with the Confucius record and the Konitz and Marsh Atlantic record?

This is difficult in retrospect. I might have some exaggerated feelings of not being comfortable and everything but I remember that was a very stimulating experience with Tristano and that rhythm section playing so respectably. That’s some of Lennie’s most relaxed playing I think.
The “Confucius” record. I felt the effects of that, too; I just have whatever complexes I bring to the mix sometimes. I’m recalling those instead of the positive part.

That was I think the first strings experience I had like that and I had deep respect for Russo’s classical-type writing. I didn’t love most of his jazz writing that much except those nice little arrangements he did for Kenton featuring a small ensemble.
But you’re a natural for a string setting. You sound [like it’s] a marriage made in heaven.
